broccoli-frozen-cooked-with-butter-or-ma.title: Broccoli, frozen, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is the edible flower head of Brassica oleracea var. italica. Frozen broccoli is quickly blanched and flash‑frozen, then cooked with butter or margarine, preserving its bright colour, crisp texture, and nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli belongs to the same family as cabbage, cauliflower, and Brussels sprouts.
Freezing after blanching retains up to 90 % of vitamin C and other antioxidants.
Butter is often used because it enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, K, C).
Broccoli is considered a “super‑vegetable” due to its high levels of vitamins, minerals, and phytochemicals.
There are over 100 broccoli varieties, but the “Calabrese” type is most commonly frozen.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Phytochemical compounds
items.content: Sulforaphane and other glucosinolates have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Fiber and minerals
items.content: Fiber promotes digestive health, while potassium and magnesium support heart and muscle function.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: A serving provides about 3 g of protein with relatively few calories.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to broccoli.

items.title: Sodium in margarine
items.content: If margarine with added salt is used, total dietary sodium should be monitored.

items.title: Possible gas formation
items.content: Broccoli can cause bloating in sensitive individuals due to raffinose.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat frozen broccoli in a skillet or microwave, adding 1‑2 tbsp butter or margarine. Season with salt, pepper, and a squeeze of lemon if desired. Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or mixed into vegetable medleys.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen broccoli in its original packaging at –18 °C. Once thawed, use within 2‑3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: An egg sandwich on a griddle or pancake is a quick, hearty breakfast consisting of eggs, toasted bread or a pancake base, often topped with cheese, ham, vegetables, and sauces. Griddle cooking gives a light crisp, while a pancake makes it soft and tender.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded egg sandwich dates back to the early 20th century when eggs became a staple in diners.
Griddle sandwiches are often made on a flat-top grill, allowing fast cooking without added oil.
Using a pancake as the “bread” became popular in the US during the 1970s as a lower‑carb alternative.
Variations with avocado, spinach, or hummus gained popularity during the health‑food movement.
Griddle sandwiches are commonly served with hash browns or a fresh side salad.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: The yolk contains B12, B2, and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Adding avocado or cheese supplies monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and complex carbs (bread or pancake) helps keep you full longer.

items.title: Vitamin D and calcium
items.content: Cheese adds calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; those with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces or processed meats can raise the sodium content.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor salmonella; cook until fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich hot, cut in half if desired. It pairs well with sliced veggies, fresh salad, ranch dressing, or mustard. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain bread or a gluten‑free pancake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat on a griddle or in the microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: The carbonated citrus fruit drink is a refreshing non‑alcoholic beverage made from a blend of citrus juices (orange, lemon, lime) and carbon dioxide. It features a bright aroma, a sweet‑tart taste, and a light fizz.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial carbonated drink appeared in the mid‑19th century.
Citrus juices are rich in vitamin C, which remains stable even after carbonation.
Carbonation enhances flavor perception, making the drink feel more “alive”.
In some countries the drink is served as “fresh shots” in small glasses.
Sugar content in the finished product can range from 5 % to 12 %.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Citrus juice provides an antioxidant that supports the immune system and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The water component helps maintain fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Mild carbonation can stimulate gastric secretions, easing digestion.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugars are rapidly absorbed, delivering an immediate source of energy.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Citrus aromas are often linked to improved mood and reduced fatigue.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive intake may contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Acids from citrus can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Some individuals experience bloating or discomfort from carbon dioxide.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to citrus components can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the drink chilled, optionally over ice or with a lemon slice to boost aroma. It works as a standalone refresher or as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Poultry gravy is a thick sauce made from the reduced stock of roasted poultry, bones, and vegetables, traditionally prepared in the early 20th century. It has a rich meaty flavor with a hint of sweetness and is used as a base for dishes or served alongside finished meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Home cooks made gravy from leftover roasted poultry, ensuring nothing went to waste.
In 1917, gravy was a staple accompaniment to festive dishes, especially roasted duck and chicken.
The classic recipe included carrots, onion, celery, and spices such as bay leaf and black pepper.
Gravy served as a base for soups and sauces as well as a flavorful topping for side dishes.
Early 20th‑century households often canned gravy in glass jars for long‑term storage.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Gravy provides a notable amount of protein derived from poultry meat, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The sauce contains iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for bones and immune function.

items.title: Contains gelatin
items.content: Bone broth in the gravy supplies gelatin, which may benefit joint health and digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Gravy delivers vitamin B12 and other B‑vitamins essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The sauce is virtually carb‑free, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared gravy can be quite salty; individuals monitoring sodium intake should use it sparingly.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to poultry proteins.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Improper storage can allow pathogenic bacteria to proliferate, so proper cooling is essential.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Traditional gravy contains saturated fats, so those with high cholesterol should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot gravy over roasted or baked poultry, use it as a base for soups, stews, and sauces. It can be thinned with water or stock for a lighter consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep gravy in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion into sterilized jars and freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Enfamil ProSobee is a ready‑to‑feed infant formula designed for babies with lactose intolerance and sensitive digestion. It contains easily digestible protein, probiotics, and an optimal blend of vitamins and minerals to support growth and development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formula is completely ready to use – no water addition required.
Includes the probiotic Bifidobacterium lactis to promote a healthy gut microbiome.
Reduced lactose content makes it suitable for infants with lactose sensitivity.
Enriched with DHA and ARA, essential fatty acids for brain and eye development.
Packaged in a 364 ml container, convenient for travel and day‑time feeding.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: Provides a balanced ratio of protein, fat, and carbohydrates along with essential vitamins and minerals for normal infant growth.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Probiotics and prebiotics help establish beneficial gut flora, reducing the risk of constipation and colic.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C, zinc, and iron strengthen the immune system, helping the baby resist infections.

items.title: Brain and eye development
items.content: DHA and ARA contribute to neural connections and visual function.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Low lactose and partially hydrolyzed protein lessen the digestive load.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Infants with a known cow‑milk protein allergy may react to this formula; a hypoallergenic alternative should be used.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: Although reduced, lactose is still present; babies with severe lactose intolerance may need a lactose‑free formula.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, the container should be used within 48 hours and kept refrigerated to prevent bacterial growth.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Do not heat the formula above 40 °C to preserve probiotic activity and nutrient integrity.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Shake the bottle before feeding, check the temperature, and give it to the baby. Do not add water, sugar, or other ingredients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and use within 48 hours.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-made-with-mayonn.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Mayonnaise

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with mayonnaise is a cold dish where cooked pasta (usually short shapes like shells, elbows, or spirals) is tossed with a mayonnaise‑based dressing, often complemented by vegetables, herbs, and spices. It is popular as a light meal for picnics, lunches, and appetizers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became a staple of American cuisine.
Traditional recipes include finely diced celery, onion, and sweet bell pepper for texture and flavor contrast.
The mayonnaise dressing can be swapped for lighter yogurt‑based versions, but the classic recipe uses regular mayo.
It is convenient to prepare ahead; the pasta holds its shape and absorbs the dressing flavors over several hours.
Different countries use local pasta types: Italy often uses farfalle, while in Russia elbow‑shaped or penne pasta is common.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The salad provides a quick source of energy from the carbohydrates in the pasta and the fats in the mayonnaise.

items.title: Protein content
items.content: Pasta contributes plant‑based protein, complementing the overall amino acid profile of the diet.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat pasta is rich in thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3), supporting metabolic processes.

items.title: Iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals in pasta help maintain normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Fiber when vegetables are added
items.content: Including fresh vegetables adds dietary fiber, which is beneficial for digestion.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: The classic mayonnaise dressing makes the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑conscious individuals.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Traditional mayo contains eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions in susceptible people.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Store‑bought mayonnaise often contains a lot of salt; low‑sodium options are recommended for those with high blood pressure.

items.title: Bacterial growth risk
items.content: The salad should be kept refrigerated and not left at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a side dish, accompaniment to meat or fish, or as a standalone meal. It can be eaten with a fork or spoon and also used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing evenly.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit pancakes are thin, pan‑fried cakes made from a batter of flour, eggs, and milk, served with a variety of fresh or baked fruits. The dish is popular in fast‑food outlets and restaurants as a quick, tasty breakfast or dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pancakes have existed in various cultures for over 5,000 years, and fruit toppings became widespread in the U.S. in the mid‑20th century.
Traditional Russian blini are cooked without leavening agents, giving them a flexible texture.
Fruits add natural sweetness, allowing the reduction of added sugar.
Pancakes are often served with butter, which helps release the aroma of the fruit.
Some eateries use whole‑grain flour for a healthier version.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The batter provides B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fruits such as apples, berries, or bananas add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berries and citrus contain vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Low saturated fat in the batter and potassium from fruits benefit vascular health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the batter and fruit quickly replenish glycogen stores for morning energy.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional batter contains wheat; people with celiac disease should use gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet fruit sauces can raise the overall sugar level, which is important for diabetics.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pancakes with butter and fruit syrup can be high in calories; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some restaurants add artificial flavorings to sauces, which may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pancakes hot, folding them into a pocket or roll and topping with fresh berries, sliced bananas, kiwi wedges, or apple sauce. A dab of butter or a swirl of yogurt adds a creamy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Keep fruit toppings separate to prevent the pancakes from becoming soggy. Reheat pancakes on a dry skillet or in the microwave before serving.

potato-salad-with-egg-made-with-light-it.title: Potato Salad with Egg, Light Italian Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: A salad made from boiled potatoes, hard‑boiled eggs, fresh vegetables and a light Italian dressing (olive oil, vinegar and herbs). It is popular in summer, has a gentle flavor and moderate calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Italian dressing often includes basil, oregano and garlic, giving the salad a Mediterranean aroma.
Traditional potato salads in many countries use mayonnaise, while the light oil‑based version is considered healthier.
Eggs add a complete protein source, making the dish more filling.
Potatoes are usually boiled with skins on to retain more nutrients.
The salad can be served chilled as an appetizer or as a side dish to meat.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and potatoes provide vitamin B6 and folate, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Skin‑on potatoes and vegetables supply dietary fiber beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The light Italian dressing is based on olive oil, which is high in monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Olive oil, basil and garlic have antioxidant properties that protect cells.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of egg protein and complex carbs from potatoes helps keep you full longer.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the dressing contains salt, monitor intake, especially for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Store the salad refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days to prevent bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone dish, as a side to fish or meat, or use it in sandwiches. Fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon can be added before serving for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Check for off‑odors or texture changes before eating; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Pretzels are crunchy snack sticks formed into knots, made from gluten‑free flour—usually rice, corn or a blend—baked to a firm crust and coated with salt or flavored seasonings. They contain no gluten, making them suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hard coated pretzels are a classic bar‑food accompaniment to beer in Germany and the United States.
Gluten‑free versions appeared in the early 2000s in response to growing demand for safe snacks.
The traditional knot symbolized intertwined hands, a medieval sign of friendship and hospitality.
More than 30 coating flavors exist, from classic salt to cheese, honey, and chili spices.
Pretzels can stay fresh for up to 6 months in a dry, cool environment if the package remains sealed.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Hard gluten‑free pretzels usually contain less fat than their soft counterparts, making them a lighter snack option.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Gluten‑free flours provide slowly released energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for individuals with celiac disease, gluten intolerance, or those following a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Corn and rice flours add modest amounts of fiber that support digestive health.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: The grains may contribute small amounts of iron, magnesium and zinc typical of whole gluten‑free cereals.

items.title: Cross‑contamination risk
items.content: Although gluten‑free, the product may contain trace amounts of wheat, barley or rye if processed on shared equipment.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Most coated pretzels are heavily salted; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Added sugars in sweet varieties
items.content: Flavors such as honey or caramel may contain added sugars.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: The hard texture can pose a choking risk for young children; supervision is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels can be enjoyed straight from the bag, paired with dips (hummus, guacamole, yogurt sauce) or tossed into salads and soups for crunch. Their long shelf life makes them convenient for travel and on‑the‑go snacking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, transfer to an airtight container. Shelf life is usually indicated on the package and ranges from 6 to 12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Tortellini are small ring-shaped pasta filled with creamy cheese. They are served with a smooth cream sauce that highlights the mild cheese flavor and makes the dish rich and satisfying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortellini originate from Italy; the name comes from the verb “torcere” meaning “to twist,” describing their shape.
Traditional fillings use ricotta, Parmesan, and sometimes spinach, while modern versions may include mozzarella, gorgonzola, or other cheeses.
Cream sauce is often made from heavy cream, butter, and Parmesan, occasionally enriched with white wine or aromatic herbs.
Tortellini are a popular festive dish because they look elegant and are easy to prepare in large quantities.
In Italy there is a regional variant called “tortellini in broth,” where the pasta is served in a light meat broth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The cheese filling provides a good source of complete protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheeses used in the filling contain calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tortellini, like most pasta, supplies B1, B2 and B3 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy‑dense cream sauce
items.content: Cream and butter add concentrated calories, useful for people with high energy needs.

items.title: Potential probiotic content
items.content: If fermented cheeses are used, they may contribute beneficial bacteria for gut health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese and cream contain lactose, so those who are intolerant should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein may react to the cheese filling.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and cheese make the dish calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Cheeses are often salty, which can increase sodium intake—caution for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional tortellini are made from wheat flour, making them unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tortellini hot, drizzled with cream sauce. Garnish with grated Parmesan, fresh herbs (basil, parsley) and a light salad. For a lighter option, use a yogurt‑based or plant‑based cream sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Dry tortellini keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months. Fresh filled tortellini store in the refrigerator for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 2 months.
